title: The Umayyad Caliphate
titleline: The Umayyad Caliphate - The History Web
para1: The Umayyad Caliphate. The Umayyad Caliphate (661-750 CE) turned the young Islamic state into one of the largest empires the world has ever seen. Founded by Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the long-serving governor of Syria who emerged victorious from Islam's first civil war, it moved the capital from Medina to Damascus and replaced the elected leadership of the Rashidun with something new: a hereditary dynasty, ruling an empire of millions - most of them not Arabs and not Muslims.
para2: The dynasty's early decades were stormy. Muawiya's son Yazid faced the revolt of Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, killed at Karbala in 680 - a wound in the community that has never healed. The Second Fitna that followed nearly destroyed the dynasty until Abd al-Malik (r. 685-705) reunified the empire by 692 and then rebuilt it: he Arabized the bureaucracy, replacing Greek and Persian with Arabic as the language of administration, minted the first distinctly Islamic coinage, and crowned his reign with the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem - the first great monument of Islamic architecture.
para3: Under Abd al-Malik's sons, above all al-Walid I, the conquests reached their astonishing peak. In a single year, 711, Umayyad armies crossed into Spain - toppling the Visigothic kingdom within a few years - and conquered Sindh in the Indus valley; in the east, others took Samarkand and Bukhara and pushed to the borders of China, while in the west the whole North African coast fell. At its height the caliphate stretched from the Atlantic to the Indus, perhaps 11 million square kilometers. It governed this vast, mostly Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist population with a light hand: the tolerated faiths paid the jizya tax and ran much of the civil service.
para4: But the empire devoured itself. Constant frontier warfare - including the great failed sieges of Constantinople - drained the treasury; Arab tribal rivalries tore the army apart; and the mawali, non-Arab converts who were Muslims yet treated as second-class citizens, provided the Abbasid revolution with its tinder. In 750 the Abbasids destroyed the dynasty at the Battle of the Zab and massacred the family. One prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped across Africa to Spain, where he founded the Emirate of Cordoba - so the Umayyad story continued for three more centuries, in the land where their conquests had reached farthest.

article.p: The Umayyad Caliphate (661-750 CE) turned the young Islamic state into one of the largest empires the world has ever seen. Its founder, Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, had served twenty years as governor of Syria when he emerged victorious from Islam's first civil war and took the caliphate in 661. He moved the capital from Medina to Damascus and replaced the elected leadership of the Rashidun with something new: a hereditary dynasty, ruling an empire of millions - most of them neither Arabs nor Muslims.

Muawiya was a politician before he was a soldier, famous for preferring gifts and patience to bloodshed. From Damascus he governed through the existing Byzantine and Sasanian machinery, kept the Arab tribal armies in uneasy balance, and built the state's first navy to raid the Byzantine frontier. But his decision to name his son Yazid as heir settled the nature of the new order: the caliphate would pass within one family. When Muawiya died in 680, the decision was tested at once.

figure.alt: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, nineteenth-century photograph
figure.cap: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed under Abd al-Malik in 691-692 - the first great monument of Islamic architecture. Photograph by the Bonfils studio, nineteenth century. Public domain.

article.p: Yazid's reign brought the dynasty's darkest hour: the revolt of Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, ended with his death at Karbala in 680 - a wound in the community that has never healed. The Second Fitna that followed nearly destroyed the Umayyads; rival authority held Mecca, and the dynasty's survival hung by a thread. It was saved by Abd al-Malik (r. 685-705), who reunified the empire by 692 and then rebuilt it deliberately: he replaced Greek and Persian with Arabic as the language of administration, minted the first distinctly Islamic coinage, and crowned his reign with the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem - the announcement, in stone and mosaic, that Islam had an empire to match its faith.

Under Abd al-Malik's sons, above all al-Walid I, the conquests reached their astonishing peak. In a single year, 711, Umayyad forces crossed into Spain - toppling the Visigothic kingdom within a few years - and conquered Sindh in the Indus valley. In the east other armies took Samarkand and Bukhara and pushed toward the borders of China; in the west the whole North African coast fell, and in the Mediterranean the caliphate's fleets fought the Byzantines for the sea. At its height the empire stretched from the Atlantic to the Indus - perhaps eleven million square kilometers. It governed this vast, mostly Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist population with a light hand: the tolerated faiths paid the jizya tax and staffed much of the civil service.

figure.cap: The Caliphate in 750, at the end of Umayyad rule: the conquests up to 632, under the first three caliphs to 656, and under the Umayyads, 661-750. From William Shepherd's Historical Atlas (1923). Public domain.

article.p: The same expansion destroyed the dynasty. Constant frontier warfare - above all the great failed sieges of Constantinople - drained the treasury; the Arab tribal factions within the army tore at each other; and the mawali, the non-Arab converts who were Muslims yet treated as second-class citizens, gave the opposition its tinder. In the east a revolution gathered under the banner of the Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet's uncle Abbas, and in 750 it destroyed the dynasty at the Battle of the Zab. The victors massacred the Umayyad family, even exhuming the caliphs from their tombs.

One prince escaped. Abd al-Rahman, a grandson of the caliph Hisham, fled across North Africa one step ahead of Abbasid agents and crossed into Spain - the farthest reach of his family's conquests. There, in 756, he was proclaimed emir and founded the Emirate of Cordoba, which under his descendants would become the most brilliant state in Europe. The Umayyads had lost their empire in the east; in the west their story ran for three more centuries.

title: The Uyghur Khaganate
titleline: The Uyghur Khaganate - The History Web
para1: The Uyghur Khaganate. The Uyghur Khaganate (744-840) ruled the steppe for a century between the Göktürks and the Mongols - and it broke the steppe's oldest rule, for the Uyghurs built cities. Calling themselves the Toquz Oghuz, the Nine Tribes, they rose in 744 when a Uyghur-Karluk alliance destroyed the Basmyls who had toppled the Second Göktürk Khaganate; the next year they killed the last Göktürk khagan and sent his head to the Tang emperor. From their capital at Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon - a walled city on the open steppe - the Uyghur khagans ruled, in the words of the Tang histories, 'the entire territory of the ancient Xiongnu'.
para2: The Uyghurs built their empire on an unusual foundation: not raiding China but rescuing it. When the An Lushan rebellion nearly destroyed the Tang dynasty in 755, it was Uyghur cavalry that retook the capitals Chang'an and Luoyang - and the Uyghurs collected their price in silk: tens of thousands of rolls a year, a horse trade fixed at forty rolls of silk per horse, marriage alliances with Tang princesses, and 'guest' status for Uyghurs in China. When the Tang retreated from Central Asia after their defeat by the Arabs at Talas in 751, the Uyghurs were left the dominant power of the Silk Road, and Sogdian merchants flocked to their court.
para3: In 762 the khagan Bögü, campaigning in China, encountered Manichaean priests - and converted. It was an astonishing choice: a steppe empire adopting, as its state religion, the Persian faith of light and darkness, a religion of books and merchants rather than warriors. The khaganate's official religion became Manichaeism, practiced alongside Tengrism, Buddhism, and Nestorian Christianity - an empire of unusual religious diversity even by steppe standards.
para4: The end came with terrible speed. Famine, epidemic, and a killing winter in 839-840 gutted the herds the empire lived on, and in 840 the Yenisei Kyrgyz - invited in by a rebellious Uyghur minister - swept down with 80,000 horsemen, sacked and burned Ordu-Baliq, and destroyed the khaganate in a single campaign. The Uyghurs fled south and west as refugees; in the oases of Gansu and the Tarim Basin they built new states, the Gansu Uyghur Kingdom and the Kingdom of Qocho, that carried Uyghur culture on for centuries.

title: The Western Xia, Liao, & Jin Dynasties
titleline: The Western Xia, Liao, & Jin Dynasties - The History Web
para1: The Western Xia, Liao, and Jin Dynasties. Between the fall of the Tang and the rise of the Mongols, northern China was ruled not by Chinese dynasties but by three great conquest empires of steppe peoples: the Khitan Liao, the Tangut Western Xia, and the Jurchen Jin. Each blended nomadic power with Chinese government, and together they held the north for three centuries while the Song ruled the south.
para2: The first were the Khitans, a nomadic people of the northeast. In 907 their leader Abaoji became khagan; in 916 he took the title of emperor and founded the Liao dynasty (916-1125). The Liao created a remarkable dual state: a Northern Administration ruling the steppe tribes in the old nomadic way, and a Southern Establishment governing the settled Chinese population on Tang models, with its own Khitan scripts invented for the purpose. In 1005 the Chanyuan Treaty settled peace with the Song on equal terms. So dominant were the Khitans that their name - Khitai - became the word for China itself across Central Asia and Russia, reaching Europe as 'Cathay.'
para3: To the west, the Tanguts - a people of the northwest borderlands - proclaimed the Western Xia (1038-1227), ruling a million square kilometers of north-central China from their capital at Xingqing (modern Yinchuan). Buddhist and Confucian by turns, they created their own intricate script and held off both Song and Liao for two centuries. Their end was terrible: the Western Xia was annihilated by the Mongols in 1227, its records and architecture so thoroughly destroyed that its history was nearly lost until 20th-century scholarship recovered it.
para4: The third conquest came from the Jurchens, subject tribes of the Liao who rebelled under Aguda, who founded the Jin dynasty in 1115. The Jin destroyed their Liao overlords in 1125 - the Liao remnant fleeing west to found the Qara Khitai in Central Asia - then broke their Song allies, capturing Kaifeng, two emperors, and the entire northern heartland in the Jingkang catastrophe of 1127. The Jin ruled north China for over a century, from Manchuria to the Huai River, until the Mongols ground them down and took their last refuge at Caizhou in 1234. The steppe's three empires had proven that nomads could rule China; the Mongols were about to prove they could rule all of it.

title: The Yuan Dynasty
titleline: The Yuan Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Yuan Dynasty. The Yuan dynasty (1271-1368) was China's first empire under foreign rule - the moment when the heirs of Genghis Khan ceased to be merely conquerors of China and became its emperors. In 1271 Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis and Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, proclaimed the 'Great Yuan' in the Chinese style, taking the name from the I Ching and claiming the Mandate of Heaven and the succession of China's dynasties. In 1279 his forces destroyed the last Song resistance at the naval Battle of Yamen, and for the first time in history a non-Han dynasty ruled all of China proper.
para2: Kublai (r. 1260-1294) built a new capital at Dadu - modern Beijing - with a summer capital at Shangdu in the steppe. The Yuan empire was, in name, the supreme khanate of the Mongol world: the western khans formally recognized the Yuan emperor's supremacy in 1304, though in practice each khanate went its own way. The dynasty governed a vast multi-ethnic state, kept Mongolian written in the new 'Phags-pa script alongside Chinese, and circulated paper money across the empire.
para3: The Yuan century left deep marks on China: Beijing's career as the national capital began at Dadu, and the Pax Mongolica's open roads brought unprecedented contact between China and the world of Islam and Europe. Yet Mongol rule never fully took root. The emperors after Kublai grew weaker, and the dynasty's century closed in flood, famine, and rebellion: the Red Turban revolts that began in 1351 devoured the south, and in 1368 the rebel leader Zhu Yuanzhang drove the court from Dadu and proclaimed the Ming dynasty.
para4: The Yuan story did not quite end there: the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian plateau and ruled on as the 'Northern Yuan' until 1635. But in Chinese history, 1368 closed a unique chapter - the era when the steppe ruled the sown, and the world's largest land empire had its heart on the site of Beijing.

article.p: The Yuan dynasty (1271-1368) was China's first empire under foreign rule - the moment when the heirs of Genghis Khan ceased to be merely conquerors of China and became its emperors. In 1271 Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis and Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, proclaimed the 'Great Yuan' in the Chinese style, taking the name from the I Ching and claiming the Mandate of Heaven and the succession of China's dynasties. In 1279 his forces destroyed the last Song resistance at the naval battle of Yamen, and for the first time in history a non-Han dynasty ruled all of China proper - unifying the country for the first time since the ninth century.

figure.alt: Portrait of Kublai Khan from the Yuan imperial album
figure.cap: Kublai Khan - from the Yuan dynasty's own album of imperial portraits, painted at his court. Public domain.

article.h2: The Long War with the Song

article.p: The conquest took eleven years of grinding siege warfare. The Song countered the Mongol cavalry with fortified cities and rivers, and Kublai picked off the strongpoints one by one - most famously Xiangyang, which held out for six years. In 1276 the empress dowager surrendered the Song capital Lin'an with the child emperor Gongzong; loyalists fought on with two more boy emperors until the Mongol fleet caught them at Yamen, near modern Macao, on 19 March 1279. The last Song chancellor leapt into the sea with the nine-year-old Emperor Bing in his arms, and the Song were finished. Kublai's ambitions were not: his two invasions of Japan failed, wrecked by storms the Japanese called kamikaze, the 'divine wind', and his expeditions into Southeast Asia fared little better.

figure.alt: Kublai Khan hunting, painted by Liu Guandao in 1280
figure.cap: Kublai hunting in the steppe with his court - the emperor in the white ermine coat at center - by the court painter Liu Guandao, 1280. Public domain.

article.p: Kublai (r. 1260-1294) built a new winter capital at Dadu - modern Beijing - with a summer capital at Shangdu, 'Xanadu', in the steppe: the twin cities summed up the dynasty's double nature, Chinese empire and Mongol khanate at once. The Yuan was, in name, the supreme khanate of the Mongol world, and in 1304 the western khans formally recognized the Yuan emperor's supremacy, though in practice each khanate went its own way. The dynasty governed a vast multi-ethnic state with Mongols and foreigners - Persians, Central Asians, even the Venetian Marco Polo claimed a place at court - in the top ranks; it commissioned the 'Phags-pa script to write Mongolian and circulated paper money across the empire. The open roads of the Pax Mongolica brought unprecedented contact between China, the Islamic world and Europe, and Beijing's career as China's capital began at Dadu.

article.h2: Flood, Famine and the Red Turbans

article.p: Mongol rule never fully took root. The emperors after Kublai grew weaker, the court tore itself in succession struggles, and the government overspent and overtaxed while Yellow River floods and famine battered the countryside. Peasant revolts rumbled through the fourteenth century until the Red Turban rebellions, beginning in 1351, devoured the south. Out of the chaos rose Zhu Yuanzhang, a destitute peasant turned monk turned rebel commander; in 1368 he drove the Mongol court from Dadu and proclaimed the Ming dynasty.

The Yuan story did not quite end there. The Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian plateau and ruled on as the 'Northern Yuan' until 1635. But in Chinese history 1368 closed a unique chapter: the era when the steppe ruled the sown, when the world's largest land empire had its heart on the site of Beijing - and when China, for one century, was the greatest prize of the house of Genghis Khan.

title: The Ayyubid Sultanate
titleline: The Ayyubid Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Ayyubid Sultanate (1171-1250) was the Kurdish dynasty that turned Egypt into the sword-arm of the counter-crusade. Its founder was Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub - Saladin to the West - whose father Ayyub and uncle Shirkuh were Kurdish soldiers of fortune from Dvin in Armenia who rose in service to the Zengid rulers of Syria. When Shirkuh's armies marched into a Fatimid Egypt torn by palace intrigue, his nephew went with them, and in 1169 Saladin became vizier to the last Fatimid caliph while commanding the Syrian army of occupation.
para2: In 1171 Saladin quietly ended two centuries of Shi'a Fatimid rule, restoring Egypt to Sunni Islam and the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad; when his old master Nur al-Din died in 1174, he took Damascus and gathered Muslim Syria around him. Then came the confrontation that made his name: at Hattin in 1187 he destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and retook the city itself, ending 88 years of crusader rule. The Third Crusade answered, Richard the Lionheart clawed back the coast, but the Treaty of Jaffa in 1192 left Jerusalem Muslim - and Saladin's restraint in victory made him the medieval world's model of chivalrous kingship.
para3: The sultanate did not remain one man's empire for long. Saladin had divided his lands among his sons and his brother al-Adil, and after his death in 1193 the dynasty became a family federation of princes in Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Hama, Homs and the Jazira. Al-Adil (r. 1200-1218) mastered it by placing the great appanages in the hands of his own sons; his son al-Kamil (r. 1218-1238) survived the Fifth Crusade's siege of Damietta and in 1229 peacefully ceded Jerusalem to Emperor Frederick II. When al-Kamil died the family wars resumed, until al-Salih Ayyub (r. 1240-1249) began wrenching Egypt into a centralized state run not by kinsmen but by his own slave-soldiers, the Bahri mamluks.
para4: It was those mamluks who buried the dynasty. When al-Salih died in 1249, within a year his Bahri regiment had murdered his son Turanshah and seized the throne. The Syrian branches fell to the Mongols in 1260 and were absorbed into the Mamluk Sultanate, though Ayyubid princes lingered in Hama until 1341 and, under Mongol and Turkmen overlords, in little Hisn Kayfa until 1462. The dynasty's legacy outlasted its politics: the madrasas it planted in Egypt and Jerusalem, the Citadel of Cairo, the defenses of Aleppo - and the memory of Saladin, for eight centuries the benchmark of Muslim kingship.

title: The Ghaznavid Empire
titleline: The Ghaznavid Empire - The History Web
para1: The Ghaznavid Empire. The Ghaznavid Empire (977-1186) was the first great Turko-Persian sultanate, founded by Sabuktigin, a Turkic slave-soldier (mamluk) who seized the governorship of Ghazna (in modern Afghanistan) from his Samanid masters. His son Mahmud of Ghazna (r. 998-1030) made it an empire: from his Afghan capital he ruled Khorasan, Afghanistan, and at his peak much of Iran, and he became the most feared conqueror of his age for his seventeen expeditions into India.
para2: Mahmud's Indian campaigns - against the Hindu Shahis, the cities of the Punjab, and deep raids as far as Kannauj, Mathura and the fabulously rich temple of Somnath (1025-26) - carried off immense plunder and annexed the Punjab permanently to an Islamic state, the opening wedge of Muslim rule in northern India. His enemies remembered him as an idol-smasher; his own court remembered him as a ghazi champion of Sunni Islam, recognized by the Abbasid caliph and hostile to the Shi'a Buyids and Ismailis alike.
para3: Mahmud spent his plunder on culture. Ghazna was briefly one of the intellectual capitals of the Islamic world: the poet Firdawsi dedicated the Shahnameh, the Persian national epic, to him (and was famously disappointed by his reward); the great polymath al-Biruni, taken from Khwarazm, wrote his celebrated study of India at the Ghaznavid court; and historians like al-Utbi and Bayhaqi chronicled the empire in Persian and Arabic. The dynasty's patronage decisively established New Persian as the literary language of the eastern Islamic world.
para4: Mahmud's son Mas'ud lost the western half of the empire to the Seljuk Turks at Dandanqan (1040), and the later Ghaznavids ruled on in Afghanistan and the Punjab, moving their capital to Lahore, until the Ghurids took Ghazna (1150) and finally Lahore (1186). Their legacy: Persianate Islamic civilization planted permanently in India, where Lahore and Delhi would inherit it.

title: The Ghurid Sultanate
titleline: The Ghurid Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Ghurid Sultanate. The Ghurids (c. 1011-1215) were a mountain dynasty from Ghur, the remote highlands of central Afghanistan, who rose from local chiefs - first as tribute-payers, then rivals, of the Ghaznavids - to build the last great empire of the eastern Islamic world before the Mongols. The dynasty's rise began with a family feud: after the Ghaznavid sultan poisoned their prince, his brother Ala al-Din Husain 'World-Burner' (Jahansuz) sacked Ghazna itself in 1150, and his nephews Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad and Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (Muhammad of Ghor) divided and expanded the realm.
para2: While Ghiyath al-Din ruled the west from Firuzkuh, Mu'izz al-Din turned east and changed Indian history. After an early defeat by the Rajput confederacy of Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1191), he returned the next year and crushed the Rajputs at the second battle of Tarain (1192), opening the Gangetic plain. His slave-generals - Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bakhtiyar Khalji - took Delhi, sacked the great Buddhist university of Nalanda, and carried Turkish arms to Bengal; defeated in turn by the Khwarazmians at Andkhud (1204), Mu'izz al-Din was assassinated in 1206, and his Indian conquests became the independent Delhi Sultanate under Aibak.
para3: In their heyday the Ghurids ruled from Herat to the Bay of Bengal and built some of the most beautiful monuments of the age: the minaret and palace of Firuzkuh, the surviving Minaret of Jam - a 65-meter tower of carved brick and Kufic inscription, now a UNESCO World Heritage site - and the great mosques of Ghazna and Delhi begun by their generals, including Delhi's Qutb Minar, finished by the Delhi sultans.
para4: The empire had no deep roots: held together by the two brothers' energy, it was squeezed between the Khwarazmian Empire and its own rebellious generals, and after 1210 the Khwarazmshah Muhammad overran it; the last Ghurid holdings fell by 1215. But their Indian inheritance, the Delhi Sultanate, ruled for another three centuries.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Firuzkuh: The Ghurid Capital

title: The Khwarazmian Empire
titleline: The Khwarazmian Empire - The History Web
para1: The Khwarazmian Empire. The Khwarazmians (c. 1077-1231) rose from governors of Khwarazm, the oasis region on the lower Oxus (Amu Darya) south of the Aral Sea, first serving the Seljuks and then the Kara Khitai. Under Ala al-Din Tekish (r. 1172-1200) and above all his son Ala al-Din Muhammad II (r. 1200-1220), they shook off their overlords, conquered the Ghurid lands, Khorasan and most of Iran, and briefly ruled the largest Islamic empire of the age, from the borders of Iraq to India and the Syr Darya.
para2: Muhammad's empire was vast but brittle: freshly conquered, riven by the rivalry between the sultan and his formidable mother Terken Khatun, whose Qipchaq troops terrorized his subjects, and at odds with the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, whom Muhammad threatened to depose. When Mongol trade envoys were killed at Otrar in 1218 by his governor - and Genghis Khan's ambassadors then humiliated - Muhammad chose defiance rather than handing over the culprit.
para3: Genghis Khan's invasion of 1219-1221 was the catastrophe of the age. Muhammad scattered his army in city garrisons, which the Mongols destroyed piece by piece: Bukhara, Samarkand, Otrar, Gurganj (the Khwarazmian capital) and the cities of Khorasan - Merv, Nishapur, Herat - were stormed and devastated with enormous loss of life. The sultan fled across Iran and died, broken, on a Caspian island in 1220; his son Jalal al-Din Mangburni fought a brilliant guerrilla war, won at Parwan, but was defeated on the Indus (1221) and spent a decade as a fugitive warlord in the west before being killed in 1231.
para4: The fall of Khwarazm marked the real beginning of the Mongol domination of the Islamic world: eastern Iran never fully recovered from the destruction, the irrigation systems of Khorasan lay ruined for generations, and the road stood open to the sack of Baghdad a generation later.
source2label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Khwarazmshahs: The Line of Anustigin
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Chorasmia in Islamic Times

title: The Zengid Dynasty
titleline: The Zengid Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Zengid Dynasty. The Zengids (1127-1222) were a Turkish dynasty of Syria and the Jazira (Upper Mesopotamia) who led the Muslim counter-offensive against the Crusader states. The founder, Imad al-Din Zengi, a Seljuk officer, took Mosul in 1127 and then Aleppo, uniting northern Syria and the Jazira under one strong ruler for the first time in the Crusading era and using the ideology of jihad to bind his Turkish soldiers and Arab subjects together.
para2: Zengi's masterstroke came in 1144, when he stormed Edessa, the first and most exposed of the Crusader principalities - the shock that provoked the Second Crusade in Europe. Murdered by a servant in 1146, he was succeeded by his son Nur al-Din (r. 1146-1174), who ruled from Aleppo and Damascus, destroyed the Second Crusade's hopes, and completed the encirclement of the Crusader states by taking Egypt: his Kurdish general Shirkuh and Shirkuh's nephew Saladin seized Cairo in 1169, ending Fatimid rule.
para3: Nur al-Din built more than an army: his network of madrasas (Nur al-Din is remembered as the great patron of Sunni madrasas and the first hospital of Damascus), his care for Sunni orthodoxy, and his reputation for justice made him a model Muslim ruler, and his court crafted the public ideology of the Counter-Crusade - uniting the Muslim world for jihad - that Saladin would inherit. On his death his Syrian lands fell to Saladin, who married his widow and took Damascus (1174), while his heirs held Mosul and the Jazira under Saladin's overlordship.
para4: The dynasty's descendants clung to Mosul and the Jazira towns as Ayyubid vassals until the line died out there in 1222. Their historical role was pivotal: Zengi and Nur al-Din broke the Crusaders' security, retook Egypt, and made possible Saladin's victory at Hattin.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Zengids & the Crusaders
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Atabak

title: The Abbasid Caliphate
titleline: The Abbasid Caliphate - The History Web
para1: The Abbasid Caliphate. The Abbasid Caliphate (750-1258), second of the two great caliphal dynasties, was founded on revolution: the descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas, riding a wave of discontent in Khorasan among converts (mawali) and Shi'a sympathizers, overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and massacred the fallen house. The new caliphs - al-Saffah, then al-Mansur - moved the center of the Islamic world east to Iraq, founding Baghdad (762), the 'City of Peace', soon the largest city on earth.
para2: The early Abbasid century - Harun al-Rashid (786-809) and his son al-Ma'mun (813-833) - was the golden age of Islamic civilization. Baghdad's House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) translated Greek, Persian and Indian learning into Arabic; al-Khwarizmi gave mathematics algebra and algorithms; the court of the Thousand and One Nights set the literary imagination of the world. But the empire was already fraying: civil war between al-Amin and al-Ma'mun (809-813) shattered Iraq, provincial dynasties (Tahirids, Saffarids, Samanids) peeled away, and from 836 the caliphs became prisoners of their own Turkish slave-soldiers at Samarra.
para3: From 945 the caliphs lost all temporal power, reigning as religious figureheads under successive protectors - the Shi'a Buyids (945-1055), then the Sunni Seljuks (1055-1194) - while rival caliphates rose in Cairo and Cordoba. Yet the Abbasid name retained enormous spiritual authority: every Sunni ruler sought the caliph's investiture, and al-Nasir (r. 1180-1225) briefly rebuilt real power in Iraq.
para4: In 1258 the Mongol Hulegu stormed Baghdad, sacked the city and executed the caliph al-Musta'sim, ending the classical caliphate. The Mamluks of Egypt sheltered an Abbasid shadow-caliphate in Cairo until 1517, but the Baghdad caliphate's five centuries - above all its fusion of Persian statecraft, Greek science and Arabic-Islamic culture - remained the standard against which the whole Islamic world measured legitimacy and civilization.
source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Abbasid Period (750-1258)
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: The Abbasid Empire

title: The Hamdanid Dynasty
titleline: The Hamdanid Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Hamdanid Dynasty. The Hamdanids (890-1004) were an Arab dynasty of the Taghlib tribe who ruled the Jazira (Upper Mesopotamia) and northern Syria in the 10th century, when Abbasid power had collapsed. From their first seat at Mosul, the family produced the century's most famous warrior-princes: Nasir al-Dawla, who ruled the Jazira from Mosul, and his brother Sayf al-Dawla ('Sword of the State'), who took Aleppo in 944 and made it the capital of a warrior court on the Byzantine frontier.
para2: Sayf al-Dawla (r. 944-967) spent his reign in annual holy war against Byzantium - celebrated raids deep into Anatolia alternating with devastating defeats as the resurgent empire of Nikephoros Phokas and John Tzimiskes retook Crete, Cilicia and finally Aleppo itself (962), which was sacked. But his court made Aleppo an Arab cultural capital: the great poet al-Mutanabbi wrote his most famous panegyrics for Sayf al-Dawla, the philosopher al-Farabi found refuge there, and the historian-poet Abu Firas, his cousin, immortalized the frontier wars in verse.
para3: The Hamdanid state was a family confederation - Mosul, Aleppo, and the Jaziran towns held by cousins - held together by tribal levies and frontier ghazi volunteers, chronically short of money and squeezed between Byzantium, the Buyids of Baghdad, the Fatimids of Egypt and their own rebellious soldiers. After Sayf al-Dawla's death his heirs held Aleppo with diminishing independence under Fatimid suzerainty until 1004, when the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ended the line; the Mosul branch had already fallen to the Uqaylids in 991.
para4: The Hamdanids' century is remembered less for state-building than for a brilliant Indian summer of Arab letters - al-Mutanabbi, al-Farabi, Abu Firas - on the eve of the Turkish and Crusader eras, and for the frontier epic of Sayf al-Dawla, the last Arab warrior-prince of medieval Syria.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Nikephoros II Phokas
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: The Fatimid Caliphate

title: The Saffarid Dynasty
titleline: The Saffarid Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Saffarid Dynasty. The Saffarids (861-1003) were the first of the new Iranian dynasties to break the Abbasid order by force, and their founder's story is one of the most remarkable rises of the age: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, a coppersmith (saffar) from Sistan (southeastern Iran), began as the leader of an 'ayyar vigilante band fighting the Kharijites, was made governor of Sistan by the caliph's governor of Khorasan, and in 861 set out to build an empire of his own.
para2: Ya'qub conquered with startling speed: all of Sistan and Kerman, then Fars, and in 873 he took Nishapur and ended the Tahirid dynasty, bringing Khorasan under his rule. Twice he marched on Baghdad itself to claim the caliphate's heartland, and only a decisive Abbasid victory at Dayr al-Aqul (876), led by the caliph's brother al-Muwaffaq, stopped him. He died in 879, still ruling everything east of Iraq.
para3: His brother Amr (r. 879-901) ruled more cautiously, accepting investiture from the caliph, but overreached in 900 by challenging the Samanids for Transoxiana: defeated and captured at Balkh, he was sent in chains to Baghdad and executed. Thereafter the Saffarids shrank back to their Sistan homeland, surviving for another century as local rulers - sometimes Samanid, sometimes Ghaznavid vassals - until the line ended around 1003.
para4: The Saffarids matter beyond their brief empire: they proved that eastern Iranian rulers could defy Baghdad, opening the age of the Iranian successor dynasties; their court revived New Persian poetry - Ya'qub was among the first rulers praised in Persian verse - and their Sistan homeland preserved a distinct Iranian-Islamic frontier culture, celebrated in the epic traditions of the Shahnameh.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ya'qub b. Layth b. Mo'addal

title: The Samanid Empire
titleline: The Samanid Empire - The History Web
para1: The Samanid Empire. The Samanids (819-999) were an Iranian dynasty from the village of Saman near Balkh whose four grandsons were rewarded by the Abbasids with governorships in Transoxiana for supporting the caliph al-Ma'mun. From those beginnings they built the last and greatest of the eastern Iranian empires: Isma'il ibn Ahmad (r. 892-907) united Transoxiana and Khorasan, destroyed the Saffarid empire by capturing Amr al-Layth at Balkh (900), and ruled from Bukhara a realm stretching from the Oxus to the borders of India and Iraq.
para2: Samarkand and especially Bukhara became under the Samanids the cultural capitals of the eastern Islamic world. Their court consciously revived Persian letters: Rudaki, the blind court poet, founded the classical Persian poetic tradition; Daqiqi and the young Firdawsi began the work that became the Shahnameh; and the vizier Bal'ami produced the Persian adaptation of Tabari's great history. Scientists like the young Ibn Sina (Avicenna), who used the Samanid royal library, and geographers like al-Istakhri flourished under their protection.
para3: The Samanids were also the frontier state of Islam in Central Asia: their ghazis raided the pagan Turks, their merchants and missionaries converted them, and Turkish slave-soldiers from the steppe entered Samanid service in growing numbers - the same institution that would produce the Ghaznavids and, in part, their own undoing. Nominally loyal to the Abbasid caliph, the Samanids were in practice fully independent monarchs who combined Iranian kingship with Sunni orthodoxy.
para4: From mid-century court factions of Turkish generals and rival emirs hollowed out the state, and the end came quickly: in 999 the Qarakhanid Turks took Bukhara without a battle while Mahmud of Ghazna absorbed Khorasan. But the Samanid century had fixed the Persian language and Persianate culture of the Islamic east - the foundation on which every later dynasty from the Ghaznavids to the Mughals would build.
source2label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Khorasan in the Taherid and Samanid Periods
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Esma'il b. Ahmad Samani

title: The Tahirid Dynasty
titleline: The Tahirid Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Tahirid Dynasty. The Tahirids (821-873) were the first hereditary dynasty of the Abbasid era and the model for all that followed. Their founder, Tahir ibn al-Husayn, was the general who won the great civil war (809-813) for the caliph al-Ma'mun, commanding his Khorasanian army at the siege of Baghdad; his reward was the governorship of Khorasan in 821, with its capital at Nishapur, and when he died suddenly the next year, the caliph let his son Talha inherit - an unprecedented concession of hereditary rule.
para2: For half a century the Tahirids ruled Khorasan and the east - Transoxiana, Sistan, and the frontiers of the steppe - with practical independence: they omitted the caliph's name from the Friday prayer until warned, appointed their own officials, and kept their own army, while sending regular tribute and the caliph's gifts of investiture flowed back east. Tahir's descendants also supplied the caliphs with their other pillar of power in the west: the Tahirid Ishaq and his heirs commanded the security (shurta) of Baghdad itself for decades.
para3: The dynasty's rule is remembered as a golden interlude of order: Nishapur flourished as a center of Sunni scholarship and trade, irrigation and agriculture were maintained, and the frontier war against the steppe was pressed by Tahirid governors. But as the Samarra caliphate slid into military anarchy, the dynasty's grip loosened, and in 873 the coppersmith-adventurer Ya'qub al-Saffar took Nishapur almost unopposed, ending Tahirid rule.
para4: The Tahirids' historical significance is structural: they established the pattern of the hereditary, nominally caliph-loyal provincial dynasty through which the Abbasid Empire would actually be governed for two centuries - the pattern the Saffarids, Samanids, and ultimately the Seljuks and their atabegs would follow.

source3label: Britannica: Saffarid dynasty

title: The Qarakhanids
titleline: The Qarakhanids - The History Web
para1: The Qarakhanids. The Qarakhanids (999-1211) were the first Turkic Muslim dynasty to rule Central Asia. Descended from the Karluk and related tribes of the western steppe, whose ruler Satuq Bughra Khan had converted to Islam in the mid-10th century, they ended Samanid rule in 999 when the Ilak (Ilig) Nasr took Bukhara, and went on to rule Transoxiana, Kashgaria and the Tarim Basin for two centuries.
para2: The dynasty never formed a single centralized empire: it split (formally by the 1040s) into a western khanate at Samarkand and Bukhara and an eastern one at Kashgar and Balasagun, ruled by rival branches of the family under the supreme title of khaqan (khan of khans). Their most celebrated ruler, Tamghach Khan Ibrahim (r. 1052-1068), restored prosperity after civil wars; but from 1089 the western khanate fell under Seljuk overlordship, and in the 12th century the whole dynasty became a tributary of the Kara Khitai.
para3: Qarakhanid rule transformed the culture of Central Asia. Under them, Turkic peoples of the oases and steppe adopted Islam and Persianate urban civilization, while a new Islamic-Turkic literature was born: Yusuf Khass Hajib wrote the Kutadgu Bilig ('Wisdom of Royal Glory', 1069), the first great work in a Turkic language, for the Qarakhanid prince of Kashgar, and Mahmud al-Kashgari compiled his famous dictionary of the Turkic dialects (1072-74). Their madrasas, caravanserais, and the stunning brick minarets of Bukhara (the Kalyan Minaret, 1127, spared by Genghis Khan) and Uzgen survive today.
para4: Squeezed between the Kara Khitai, the Khwarazmians and the rebellious Kuchlug, the last Qarakhanid khans of Samarkand and Kashgar were extinguished by 1211-1212. But they had made Islam permanently Turkic and Central Asia permanently Muslim, and their blend of Turkic kingship and Persian-Islamic culture defined the region until the Mongols and long after.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Central Asia in the Islamic Period up to the Mongols

title: The Rasulid Dynasty of Yemen
titleline: The Rasulid Dynasty of Yemen - The History Web
para1: The Rasulid Dynasty of Yemen. The Rasulids (1229-1454) ruled Yemen for two centuries as heirs of the Ayyubids, whose governor Nur al-Din Umar - a Turkic mamluk commander - stayed on as an independent sultan when the Egyptian overlords withdrew. From capitals at Zabid and Ta'izz, the Rasulids built what historians often call medieval Yemen's golden age: a stable, wealthy kingdom controlling both the highlands and the coasts of Arabia's southwest corner.
para2: Rasulid prosperity rested on Aden. The port sat where the Indian Ocean trade met the Red Sea route to Egypt, and the sultans taxed the flow of spices, textiles and horses between India, East Africa, and the Mediterranean, maintaining a fleet, ambitious diplomatic relations with the Mamluks, and a customs system that made Aden one of the busiest harbors of the 13th-15th century world - visited by the merchants whose records fill the Cairo Geniza and by travelers like Ibn Battuta.
para3: The Rasulid sultans were remarkable scholar-kings. Al-Muzaffar Yusuf I (r. 1250-1295), the dynasty's real consolidator, built madrasas and mosques across Yemen; later sultans like al-Ashraf and al-Afdal personally wrote works on astronomy, agriculture, genealogy and veterinary science, and the dynasty produced the Rasulid Hexaglot, a unique six-language dictionary (Arabic, Persian, Turkic, Mongol, Armenian and Greek) reflecting the cosmopolitan world of the Indian Ocean.
para4: After 1400 succession disputes, rebellious highland tribes, the rise of the slave-soldier commanders, and competition for Aden's trade weakened the dynasty, and in 1454 the Tahirid clan of local notables took Lahij and Aden, ending Rasulid rule. Their monuments - the mosques and madrasas of Ta'izz, Zabid and Jibla - and their scholarly legacy remain central to Yemen's medieval heritage.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Yemeni Heritage at the Met

title: The Artuqids
titleline: The Artuqids - The History Web
para1: The Artuqids. The Artuqids (1102-1409) were a Turkmen dynasty of the Anatolian frontier, founded by Artuk, a Seljuk commander rewarded with Palestine - which he promptly lost to the Crusaders. His sons and nephews did better, carving out three branches in the Diyarbakir region (Diyar Bakr) of southeastern Anatolia and the Jazira: Mardin, Hasankeyf (Amid), and Harput, which they ruled as the region's durable middle power for three centuries.
para2: Wedged between the Seljuks of Rum, the Crusader states, the Zengids, and later the Ayyubids and Mongols, the Artuqids survived by balancing: they allied with or submitted to each stronger neighbor in turn, fought for and against the Crusaders, and served as atabegs and vassals of Zengi, Saladin and the Ilkhanate in turn. Their cities - Mardin on its citadel rock, Hasankeyf on the Tigris, Diyarbakir with its black basalt walls - changed hands with them but prospered as trade and craft centers.
para3: The Artuqids' real glory is their art and architecture, among the finest of the Turkish Middle Ages: the Great Mosques of Mardin and Diyarbakir, palace carvings, and above all their figural metalwork - astonishing inlaid bronze ewers, mirrors and door fittings with courtly and astrological scenes (one carries the earliest known depiction of a Mongol court) - and their illustrated manuscripts, including copies of al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Devices with its famous automata.
para4: After Mongol overlordship the branches declined: Hasankeyf fell to the Ayyubids in 1232, Harput ended in 1334, and the Mardin line lingered as vassals until the Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen took the city in 1409. Their carved stone, metalwork and bridges - like the Malabadi Bridge - still define the landscape of southeastern Turkey.
source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Seljuq Period in Anatolia (1081-1307)
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Court and Cosmos: The Great Age of the Seljuqs

title: The Danishmendids
titleline: The Danishmendids - The History Web
para1: The Danishmendids. The Danishmendids (c. 1071-1178) were the first Turkish dynasty to rule central and eastern Anatolia after the Seljuk victory at Manzikert. Their founder, Danishmend Ghazi, about whom an entire Turkish epic romance (the Danishmendname) was later woven, established his power around Sivas, Niksar and Amasya in the decades when Turkish emirs, soldiers and nomads were streaming into the former Byzantine lands.
para2: In the generation after Manzikert the Danishmendids were often the strongest Muslim power in Anatolia, stronger than their Seljuk cousins of Rum, whom they sometimes held as near-captives. Danishmend Ghazi's son Emir Gazi Gümüshtigin captured the Crusader prince Bohemond of Antioch (1100) and destroyed two whole expeditions of the Crusade of 1101 in the Anatolian highlands - victories that closed the land route across Anatolia to western armies for a generation. Under their rule cities like Kayseri (Caesarea), Sivas and Erzurum became Turkish-Islamic centers.
para3: The dynasty's twilight came with the revival of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. Kilij Arslan II (r. 1156-1192) played the Danishmendid branches against each other, took Sivas in 1174, and by 1178 had extinguished the main line; cadet branches in Malatya and elsewhere lingered under Seljuk, then Mongol, overlordship into the 13th century.
para4: Danishmendid memory survived in epic and in stone. The Danishmendname, blending history and holy-war romance, made Danishmend Ghazi a hero of Turkish popular Islam alongside his legendary companion Battal Ghazi; and the dynasty's early mosques, tombs and the great hospital (darussifa) of Divrigi - whose carved portals, built under a later Mengujekid neighbor in the same frontier world, are UNESCO-listed - mark the first flowering of Turkish architecture in Anatolia.
source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Art of the Seljuq Period in Anatolia (1081-1307)
source3label: World History Encyclopedia: John II Komnenos

title: The Bahmani Sultanate
titleline: The Bahmani Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Bahmani Sultanate. The Bahmani Sultanate (1347-1518) was the first great Muslim kingdom of the Deccan, founded when Ala al-Din Hasan Bahman Shah, an officer of the Delhi Sultanate, led the Deccan's Muslim amirs in revolt against Muhammad bin Tughluq and made himself sultan at Gulbarga. For nearly two centuries the Bahmanis were the dominant power of peninsular India, locked in a famous long duel with the Hindu empire of Vijayanagara to their south.
para2: The sultanate's wars with Vijayanagara - over the rich Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers - were among the most savage of the age, with both sides massacring prisoners and both adopting gunpowder weapons early; the Bahmanis fielded some of India's first effective artillery. Internally the kingdom was split between the 'Deccani' old Muslim families and the 'Afaqis', newcomers from Iran and Central Asia, whose rivalry - and the over-mighty ministers it produced - ran like a fault line through Bahmani politics.
para3: The sultanate's greatest minister, Mahmud Gawan (r. 1461-1481), built the finest madrasa of the Deccan at Bidar (the new capital after 1422), extended the kingdom from sea to sea, and corresponded with the rulers of Iran - until the Deccani faction destroyed him. His murder in 1481 broke the state's cohesion, and after 1490 the provincial governors of Berar, Bidar, Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda set up as the five Deccan successor sultanates.
para4: The Bahmanis left the Deccan permanently transformed: Persian culture, gunpowder warfare, and the Indo-Islamic architecture of Gulbarga and Bidar - whose later monuments, like the madrasa of Mahmud Gawan, remain among India's finest - passed to the successor states, of which Bijapur and Golconda would outshine the parent kingdom until the Mughals came.
source2label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Islamic Art of the Deccan
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Deccan: Political and Literary History

title: The Vijayanagara Empire
titleline: The Vijayanagara Empire - The History Web
para1: The Vijayanagara Empire. The Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646) was the last great Hindu empire of South India, founded - tradition says on the advice of the sage Vidyaranya - by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family on the banks of the Tungabhadra River. From their fortress capital, the city of Vijayanagara ('City of Victory', modern Hampi), they and their successors ruled the peninsula south of the Krishna, defending and consciously reviving Hindu kingship against the Muslim sultanates of the Deccan.
para2: The empire reached its height under Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529) of the Tuluva dynasty: he humbled the Gajapatis of Orissa and the sultanate of Bijapur, took the Raichur Doab, and presided over a court where Telugu literature (the 'eight elephants' of poets) and temple-building flourished - he is still a folk hero of South India. Foreign visitors were stunned by the capital: the Portuguese travelers Paes and Nuniz described a vast city of bazaars, irrigation tanks, and temple complexes, richer than any they knew in Europe.
para3: Vijayanagara's wealth came from control of South India's trade: its ports shipped pepper, textiles and horses (bought from the Arabs and Portuguese, vital against the Deccan cavalry), and its kings built enormous irrigation works in the dry interior. Society was organized around the nayakas, warrior-governors who held land in return for military service - efficient in expansion, but a centrifugal force once royal power weakened.
para4: The end came at Talikota (1565), where the combined Deccan sultanates - Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar - crushed the imperial army, killed the regent Aliya Rama Raya, and sacked the great city, which was abandoned to become the haunting ruins of Hampi. A diminished court survived at Penukonda and Chandragiri until 1646, but the empire was over. Its nayaka heirs ruled South India for generations, and Hampi is today a UNESCO World Heritage site.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Deccan: Political and Literary History

title: The Sukhothai Kingdom
titleline: The Sukhothai Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Sukhothai Kingdom. Sukhothai (1238-1438) is remembered as the first true kingdom of the Thai people. When Angkorian Khmer power waned in the 13th century, two Thai chieftains seized the town of Sukhothai ('Dawn of Happiness') in the Chao Phraya valley in 1238, and one of their sons, Si Inthrathit, became its first king. Under his son Ramkhamhaeng the Great (r. c. 1279-1298), Sukhothai expanded to rule much of what is now Thailand and Laos, from Luang Prabang to the Malay Peninsula.
para2: Ramkhamhaeng is the culture-hero of Thai history. His famous inscription of 1292 - the earliest known writing in Thai - describes an ideal kingdom where the king sat accessible on his throne to hear any petition, trade was untaxed, 'whoever wants to trade in elephants, trades; whoever wants to trade in horses, trades', and the people lived in plenty. Whatever its idealization, the inscription records real achievements: the Thai alphabet created or codified under his patronage, the adoption of Theravada Buddhism from Ceylon, and a diplomatic court that sent embassies to Mongol China.
para3: Sukhothai's artisans produced the kingdom's enduring monuments: the temple-cities of Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai with their graceful lotus-bud chedis, and the celebrated Sukhothai school of Buddhist art - the serene walking-Buddha images, unique in world art - while its kilns exported Sawankhalok ceramics across Southeast Asia.
para4: After Ramkhamhaeng the kingdom shrank as his successors proved pious but unwarlike, and the vigorous new Thai power of Ayutthaya to the south eclipsed it: Sukhothai became its tributary in 1378 and was fully absorbed by 1438. Later Thai national memory made Sukhothai the idealized first chapter of the nation - its script, its Buddhism, and its model of the paternal Buddhist king.
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: Thai Art

title: The Dai Viet
titleline: The Dai Viet - The History Web
para1: The Dai Viet. Dai Viet ('Great Viet') was the name of the Vietnamese state from the 11th to the 18th century, centered on the Red River delta with its capital at Thang Long (Hanoi). Its classical age began when Ly Cong Uan, a commander of Buddhist temple guards, took the throne in 1009 and founded the Ly dynasty (1009-1225), which gave Vietnam its first stable, independent state structures after a thousand years of Chinese rule: a civil administration on Chinese models, a national capital at Thang Long, and official patronage of Buddhism alongside village cults.
para2: The Tran dynasty (1225-1400), which replaced the Ly by marriage and retirement-arrangement, faced the greatest test in Vietnamese history: three Mongol invasions (1258, 1285, 1287-88). Under the warrior-prince Tran Hung Dao, the Vietnamese twice drove out Kublai Khan's armies - and in 1288 annihilated his fleet at the Bach Dang River, where wooden stakes planted in the tidal channel repeated the victory won on the same river over the Chinese three centuries earlier. It was one of the very few decisive defeats of Mongol arms anywhere in the world.
para3: Classical Dai Viet balanced Chinese forms and local identity: it adopted the civil service examination, Confucian bureaucracy (the Quoc Tu Giam, the 'national university', founded 1076), and tribute diplomacy toward China, while its language, village autonomy, and martial memory remained fiercely distinct. The dynasty even projected power south, beginning the long 'nam tien' (southward advance) with wars and marriage-alliances against Champa.
para4: Weakened by court decay, the Tran were usurped in 1400 by Ho Quy Ly, whose reforms provoked a Ming invasion and occupation (1407-1427); Le Loi's ten-year resistance restored independence and founded the Later Le dynasty, whose ruler Le Thanh Tong (r. 1460-1497) codified the Hong Duc law code and destroyed Champa's power (1471). Classical Dai Viet had fixed Vietnam's territory, institutions and its pattern: Chinese-shaped state, stubbornly Vietnamese nation.
source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Vietnam Timeline

title: The Tibetan Empire
titleline: The Tibetan Empire - The History Web
para1: The Tibetan Empire. The Tibetan Empire (618-842) rose with startling speed to become one of the great powers of Asia. Its founder, Songtsen Gampo (r. c. 618-650), united the clans of the Yarlung valley, moved his capital to Lhasa, gave Tibet its written script (created by his minister Thonmi Sambhota from Indian models), and forced both Nepal and Tang China to send him royal brides - the Nepali Bhrikuti and the Chinese Wencheng, to whom Tibetan tradition credits the coming of Buddhism.
para2: Under Songtsen Gampo's successors the empire burst out of the plateau. Tibetan armies fought the Tang for the Tarim oases and the Silk Road, seized the kingdom of Gilgit, briefly occupied the Chinese capital Chang'an itself in 763 (installing a puppet emperor), and ruled an empire stretching from the Pamirs to Gansu, from the Tarim Basin to the borders of Bengal. The treaty pillar of 821-822, still standing in Lhasa, records peace between Tibet and China as equals - 'the nephew and the uncle'.
para3: The empire's court was cosmopolitan: Buddhist monks from India and China, Nestorian Christians, Manicheans and Bon priests all appear at the Tibetan court, and Tibetan documents survive from Dunhuang to Turfan. Under Trisong Detsen (r. 755-797) Buddhism became the state religion - the founding of Samye monastery (c. 779), Tibet's first, and the legendary debate at Samye between Indian and Chinese Buddhist schools decided Tibet for Indian-style Mahayana.
para4: The empire's end was sudden: the anti-Buddhist king Langdarma was assassinated in 842 and his sons' civil war shattered the realm, which fragmented into local kingdoms for four centuries. But the imperial age fixed Tibet's identity: its script, its Buddhism (revived in the 'second dissemination'), its epic memory of Songtsen Gampo, and the ruins of its royal tombs in the Yarlung valley.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Arts of the Greater Himalayas: Kashmir, Tibet, and Nepal

title: The Liao Dynasty
titleline: The Liao Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Liao Dynasty. The Liao dynasty (907-1125) was founded by the Khitans, a nomadic people of the Manchurian steppe, under Abaoji (Emperor Taizu), who proclaimed himself khan and then Chinese-style emperor - the first of the great 'conquest dynasties' that would rule North China for the following four centuries. His successors took the Sixteen Prefectures of North China (938), including modern Beijing, which became their southern capital and a Chinese metropolis for the first time under non-Chinese rule.
para2: The Liao invented a new kind of empire: dual administration. A 'northern administration' governed the Khitan and other steppe peoples by their own tribal law and customs; a 'southern administration' governed the millions of Chinese farmers by Chinese bureaucratic practice. The dynasty maintained five capitals, created Khitan large and small scripts for its language, and its emperors performed both the Chinese imperial rites and the rituals of steppe kingship - a template the Jin, Yuan and Qing would all follow.
para3: Liao China prospered: its artisans produced fine three-color (sancai) ceramics, its wooden pagodas - like the towering Sakyamuni Pagoda of Ying County (1056), the oldest and tallest wooden pagoda in the world - and its monasteries show a vigorous, conservative Buddhist culture. After a long war, the Liao and the Chinese Song dynasty made the Treaty of Chanyuan (1005): a century of peace in which Song paid annual subsidies and the two courts addressed each other as equals - a landmark in East Asian diplomacy.
para4: The dynasty was destroyed by its own vassals: the Jurchens under Aguda rebelled in 1114 and, allied with the Song, crushed the Liao by 1125. One branch fled west under Yelü Dashi and founded the Qara Khitai empire in Central Asia. The Khitan name lived on as 'Cathay' - for centuries the word for China itself in Persian, Russian and medieval Europe.
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: Hybrid States in Northern China and the Steppe

title: The Ming Treasure Voyages
titleline: The Ming Treasure Voyages - The History Web
para1: The Ming Treasure Voyages. Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming dynasty sent seven enormous naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean - the largest wooden fleets the world had ever seen. Commanded by the eunuch admiral Zheng He, a Muslim from Yunnan captured as a boy and castrated into palace service, the 'treasure fleet' numbered at its height over 300 ships and 27,000 men, led by 'treasure ships' reportedly more than 100 meters long - dwarfing anything Europe would float for centuries.
para2: The voyages were the personal project of the Yongle Emperor (r. 1402-1424), a usurper seeking legitimacy and glory abroad. The fleet's purposes mixed diplomacy, trade and power: to enroll the Indian Ocean world in China's tributary system, to display Ming might, to hunt the deposed Jianwen Emperor rumored to have fled overseas, and to bring home exotic tribute - spices, gems, ostriches, zebras, and most famously a giraffe from Malindi (1414), presented at court as the auspicious qilin of legend.
para3: Zheng He's squadrons called at Champa, Java, Malacca, Ceylon and Calicut, then Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast as far as Malindi. The fleet was no peaceful embassy only: it destroyed the pirate king Chen Zuyi at Palembang, intervened in Ceylon to seize a hostile king, and built fortified depots at Malacca and Semudera - a demonstration that China could, if it chose, command the sea lanes.
para4: After Yongle's death the voyages faced bureaucratic hostility - the cost, Confucian disdain for trade, and the renewed Mongol threat on land - and after the seventh voyage (1431-1433) they were stopped, the fleet rotted, and records were destroyed. Private Chinese trade flourished on despite sea bans, but the state's retreat from the ocean, on the eve of the Portuguese arrival, remains one of history's great 'what ifs' - and Zheng He's voyages are today celebrated in China as the high-water mark of its maritime power.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: The Seven Voyages of Zheng He
source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Yongle Emperor

title: The Shirvanshahs
titleline: The Shirvanshahs - The History Web
para1: The Shirvanshahs. The Shirvanshahs (861-1538) ruled Shirvan - the Caspian coastal plain of modern Azerbaijan - for nearly seven centuries, one of the longest-lived dynasties in Islamic history. Descended from an Arab military family Persianized over generations, they held the corridor between the Caucasus and the Caspian through every storm of the age: Sajids, Salarids, Rawadids, Seljuks, Mongols, Ilkhans, Timur, and the Qara and Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen, surviving by a practiced mix of tribute, marriage and mountain retreats.
para2: The dynasty's greatest patron-king was Ibrahim I (r. 1382-1417), and its golden age came under Khalilullah I and Farrukh Yasar in the 15th century, when Baku grew into a walled port-city and the court at Shamakhi and Baku patronized poets - the famous divan poets Khaqani and Nizami had flourished under the dynasty's earlier centuries in Shirvan, and the Shirvanshahs' protection of letters made their small kingdom a cultural beacon.
para3: The Shirvanshahs' enduring monument is Baku's old city: the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, a 15th-century complex of palace, mosque, tomb and bath of honey-colored stone, together with the mysterious Maiden Tower, forms a UNESCO World Heritage site and the emblem of Azerbaijan. Their carved stone, coinage and mosque endowments record a court that blended Persian high culture with Caspian local tradition.
para4: The end came with the Safavid revolution. The Shirvanshahs fought the fanatical Qizilbash armies of Shah Ismail I, were defeated (1500-1501), and the last ruling Shirvanshah was killed in 1538, when Shirvan became a Safavid province. The family survived as honored Safavid governors for another century - an unusually soft landing for a dynasty that had outlasted every empire it ever served.
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: The Safavid Empire

title: The Ashikaga Shogunate
titleline: The Ashikaga Shogunate - The History Web
para1: The Ashikaga Shogunate. The Ashikaga (or Muromachi) shogunate (1336-1573) was Japan's second warrior government, founded when Ashikaga Takauji turned on the emperor Go-Daigo's short-lived imperial restoration and seized Kyoto. For its first sixty years Japan had two rival courts - the Ashikaga-backed Northern Court in Kyoto and the exiled Southern Court in the Yoshino mountains - until the shogun Yoshimitsu, the regime's greatest figure, reunified them in 1392.
para2: Yoshimitsu (shogun 1368-1394, de facto ruler to 1408) made the shogunate splendid: he subdued the great provincial lords (shugo daimyo), reopened formal tribute trade with Ming China, accepting investiture as 'King of Japan', and built the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji), the gilded retreat that still symbolizes the age. Under Ashikaga patronage the Zen-linked arts that define classical Japanese culture matured: Noh theater under Zeami, the tea ceremony, ink landscape painting by monks like Sesshu, dry-landscape Zen gardens like Ryoan-ji, and the linked-verse poetry of the salons.
para3: Politically the shoguns were never masters of Japan. Real power lay with the shugo daimyo, who turned their provinces into hereditary domains, and with quarreling court factions; the shogunate's finances depended on taxing trade, temples and moneylenders. The system collapsed into the catastrophic Onin War (1467-1477) - a succession dispute that burned Kyoto to ashes and broke central authority altogether.
para4: For the next century the Ashikaga shoguns were puppets and fugitives while the daimyo fought the Sengoku wars. In 1573 the last shogun, Yoshiaki, was driven from Kyoto by Oda Nobunaga, formally ending the shogunate. Its legacy is cultural: the aesthetics of Zen - spare, asymmetrical, refined - that the world now reads as quintessentially Japanese are largely the creation of the Muromachi age.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Muromachi Period (1392-1573)

title: The Ryukyu Kingdom
titleline: The Ryukyu Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Ryukyu Kingdom. The Ryukyu Kingdom (1429-1879) united the islands of Okinawa and the Ryukyu chain into a small but extraordinary maritime state. After centuries of rival local chieftains (the 'Three Mountains' period), Sho Hashi of Chuzan conquered the island's other lords and in 1429 established his kingdom with its capital at Shuri Castle, a hilltop palace-fortress blending Chinese and Japanese forms.
para2: The kingdom's genius was trade. Wedged between China and Japan, the Ryukyus made themselves the great entrepot of the East China Sea: Ryukyuan ships carried Chinese porcelain and silk, Japanese silver and swords, Korean ginseng and Southeast Asian spices between Naha, Fuzhou, Kyushu, Siam, Malacca and Patani. Tribute missions to Ming and Qing China brought enormous trading privileges - the Ryukyuans were among the most welcome foreigners at the Chinese court - and Naha's cosmopolitan merchant community included a famous settlement of Fujianese families at Kumemura.
para3: Ryukyuan culture was distinctive: its own language and court ritual, Confucian learning, a written literature in Japanese kana and Chinese characters, the sanshin (ancestor of the Japanese shamisen), karate developed in the islands, and a religion led by priestesses (noro) under the chief priestess (kikoe-ogimi), often the king's sister. Shuri Castle's gates, with their Chinese-style calligraphy, proclaimed 'the land of propriety'.
para4: In 1609 the Satsuma domain of Japan invaded and made Ryukyu a vassal - while carefully preserving the fiction of its independence to keep the China trade flowing, a dual subordination that lasted 270 years. In 1879 the new Meiji state abolished the kingdom outright and made Okinawa a prefecture. Shuri Castle, rebuilt again and again after fire and war, remains the symbol of the islands' distinct identity.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: The Ryukyu Castles of Okinawa
source3label: Britannica: Ryukyu Islands

title: The Sultanates of Ternate and Tidore
titleline: The Sultanates of Ternate and Tidore - The History Web
para1: The Sultanates of Ternate and Tidore. Ternate and Tidore, two tiny volcanic islands in the northern Moluccas (Maluku, the 'Spice Islands' of eastern Indonesia), were for centuries among the most fought-over specks on earth: they produced nearly all the world's cloves. Their rulers converted to Islam in the 15th century - Ternate's ruler taking the title sultan around the 1480s - and built sea-going sultanates whose fleets and vassal islands stretched across the Moluccas and beyond.
para2: The two sultanates were hereditary rivals. Ternate, the stronger, reached its height under Sultan Baabullah (r. 1570-1583), 'Lord of Seventy-two Islands', whose dominion and trading networks reached from Sulawesi to Papua and whose court received European embassies. Tidore, centered on its mountain capital, drew its strength from Papuan ties and later from alliance with Spain. Between them the twin islands were the eastern anchor of the international spice routes that drew Gujarati, Javanese, Chinese and finally European ships.
para3: The Portuguese came first (1512), building a fort on Ternate and turning alliance into domination - until they murdered Ternate's Sultan Khairun, and his son Baabullah besieged and expelled them in 1575, the first major Asian victory over European power in the region. The Dutch (VOC) followed, allied with Ternate, while Spain backed Tidore from the Philippines; their proxy struggle for the clove monopoly devastated the islands, and Dutch 'extirpation' policies burned clove trees across the Moluccas to control supply.
para4: Spain withdrew in 1663, and the Dutch gradually reduced both sultanates to protected client states. But the sultanates never formally died: the Sultans of Ternate and Tidore retain their palaces and customary standing in Indonesia today - the last living heirs of the spice empire that once drew the world to two small volcanoes.

title: The Qarmatians
titleline: The Qarmatians - The History Web
para1: The Qarmatians. The Qarmatians (899-1077) were a radical Ismaili Shi'a movement that built a breakaway state in Bahrayn (eastern Arabia) and terrorized the Abbasid world for two centuries. Founded on Ismaili missionary work among the tribes and peasants of the Gulf by missionaries of the hidden Ismaili imam, the movement in Bahrayn rejected the claims of the Fatimids when they declared themselves in 909, and under Abu Tahir al-Jannabi became the scourge of Iraq and Syria.
para2: The Qarmatian state at al-Ahsa (al-Hasa), with its capital al-Mu'miniyya, was an anomaly: a communal, reportedly egalitarian society of shared property and conscript labor, run by a council of the ruling family and notables, without the usual apparatus of mosques and orthodoxy. Their power rested on Bedouin cavalry, on taxing the Gulf trade and the pilgrim routes, and on sheer terror: in 906 and again in the 920s they cut the pilgrimage caravans, and in 924-925 they reached the gates of Kufa and Basra.
para3: Their most infamous act came in 930: the Qarmatians stormed Mecca itself during the pilgrimage season, massacred pilgrims, and carried off the Black Stone of the Kaaba to al-Ahsa - an act of sacrilege that scandalized the entire Muslim world. They held it for over twenty years, returning it in 951 only after negotiations and payment, reportedly to test the Fatimid claim to be the true imams.
para4: From the later 10th century the movement faded into a local Gulf principality, fighting losing wars against the Uyunids and local tribes, and its distinct doctrine dissolved by the 11th-12th centuries. The Qarmatians remain the great heresiarch bogey of medieval Sunni and Fatimid literature alike - remembered above all for the stolen Black Stone, the darkest possible symbol of the 10th century's collapse of caliphal authority.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Hamdan Qarmat

title: The Ikhshidids and the Tulunids
titleline: The Ikhshidids and the Tulunids - The History Web
para1: The Ikhshidids and the Tulunids. The Tulunids and the Ikhshidids were the two dynasties that first detached Egypt from direct Abbasid rule. The Tulunids (868-905) began with Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkic slave-soldier sent to Egypt as lieutenant-governor, who quietly made himself its master: he built a strong army, seized Syria, stopped remitting Egypt's revenues to Baghdad, and founded a new capital, al-Qata'i, next to Fustat. His great mosque of Ibn Tulun (879), with its spiral minaret and vast brick arcades, still stands as Cairo's oldest intact monument.
para2: Ibn Tulun's son Khumarawayh (r. 884-896) ruled a brilliant, spendthrift court famous for luxury - quicksilver pools, gardens of quicksilver and scent - and married his daughter to the caliph's son in a peace settlement that recognized Tulunid hereditary rule. But the dynasty's extravagance and a child succession drained it, and in 905 an Abbasid army restored direct rule, demolishing al-Qata'i except the mosque.
para3: A generation later the pattern repeated. Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid, a Ferghana-born commander, took Egypt in 935 and Syria with it, beating off the Hamdanids; the Abbasid caliph confirmed him with the Persian title Ikhshid. His Ikhshidid dynasty (935-969) ruled Egypt for over three decades - most of them under the iron regency of his black eunuch vizier Kafur, a former slave who governed Egypt ably for twenty years and whose court poets, including the great al-Mutanabbi, both praised and mocked him.
para4: After Kafur's death in 968 the state collapsed in months: child rulers, famine, and army factions left Egypt defenseless, and in 969 the Fatimid general Jawhar marched from Ifriqiya and took the country without a battle. The Tulunid-Ikhshidid century had nonetheless decided Egypt's future: it proved Egypt could stand alone as a Mediterranean power - the reality the Fatimids, Ayyubids and Mamluks would inherit.

title: The Sulayhids of Yemen
titleline: The Sulayhids of Yemen - The History Web
para1: The Sulayhids of Yemen. The Sulayhids (1047-1138) ruled Yemen as the local champions of Fatimid Ismaili Shi'ism in the 11th-12th centuries. Their founder, Ali ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi, began as a Sunni scholar converted by the Fatimid da'wa, raised the tribes of the Haraz mountains, took Sana'a (1047) and then the lowlands, and by 1063 ruled nearly all of Yemen - capturing Aden, Jibla and even making a famous pilgrimage to Mecca at the head of an army, which briefly installed a pro-Fatimid emir there.
para2: Al-Sulayhi built a Yemeni state of unusual coherence: roads, mosques, and a new center at Dhu Jibla, where his queen - the captive-turned-wife Asma - and later his daughter-in-law presided over the court. After his murder in 1067 by the Najahids of Zabid, his son al-Mukarram Ahmad ruled nominally, but real power passed to the second queen, Arwa bint Ahmad (r. 1087-1138), one of the most remarkable women rulers in Islamic history: Sayyida Hurra, 'the Noble Lady', who governed Yemen for half a century, commanded armies, and ran the Fatimid religious mission (da'wa) for all of western India and Yemen.
para3: Queen Arwa's reign saw both splendor and schism. When the Fatimid succession split after 1094, she sided with the Tayyibi branch, making Yemen and the Indian Bohra communities the stronghold of Tayyibi Ismailism - the tradition the Dawoodi Bohras of India still follow, who revere her as their second-highest saint. Her seat at Dhu Jibla, with her mosque and tomb, remains a major pilgrimage site.
para4: After Arwa's death without heirs in 1138 the Sulayhid state dissolved into rival principalities - the Zurayids of Aden, the Mahdids of Zabid, the Hamdanids of Sana'a - until the Ayyubid conquest of 1173-74 reunified Yemen. The Sulayhid century fixed Yemen's Ismaili communities and left the two queens, Asma and Arwa, as enduring figures of Yemeni memory.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Isma'ili Literature in Persian and Arabic

title: The Muzaffarids and the Ilkhanate Successors
titleline: The Muzaffarids and the Ilkhanate Successors - The History Web
para1: The Muzaffarids and the Ilkhanate Successors. When the last Ilkhan died heirless in 1335, his empire shattered into a patchwork of successor states - and for half a century Iran was fought over by a dozen dynasties. In the west, the Jalayirids held Baghdad and Tabriz; in the northeast, the Sarbadars of Sabzevar - a remarkable radical republic of craftsmen and dervishes; in Khorasan, the Kartids of Herat, Ilkhanid vassals turned independent; and in the south, the two strongest: the Injuid house of Shiraz and Isfahan, and the Muzaffarids.
para2: The Muzaffarids (1314-1393) had begun as Arab military settlers of Khorasan under the Ilkhans. Mubariz al-Din Muhammad Muzaffar, their energetic founder, took Yazd and Kerman, then in 1353 destroyed the Injuids and seized Isfahan and Shiraz, making the family masters of southern and central Iran. His court at Shiraz briefly made the city the refuge of Persian letters - the great poet Hafez lived and wrote in Shiraz under Muzaffarid rule, protected from orthodox censors by the enlightened minister Shah Shuja.
para3: Shah Shuja (r. 1358-1386), who imprisoned his own father, was the dynasty's most capable ruler: a patron of Hafez and the historian Nizam al-Din Shami, he held Shiraz against repeated family revolts and against Timur's first advance, buying survival with tribute. But the Muzaffarids were ruined by their own ferocious family politics - Mubariz al-Din was blinded by his son, and blinding and fratricide became the dynasty's internal habit - and by Timur's rise.
para4: In 1387 Timur took Isfahan, massacring its people after they killed his collectors, and in 1393 he extinguished the Muzaffarids, blinding or executing the princes. The other successor houses fell the same way: the Kartids and Sarbadars had already submitted or been crushed, and the Jalayirids held Baghdad until Timur and then the Turkmen confederations overwhelmed them. Out of the wreckage rose Timur's empire - and later, the Safavids.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Qara Ketay

title: The Kara Khitai
titleline: The Kara Khitai - The History Web
para1: The Kara Khitai. The Kara Khitai (1124-1218), the 'Black Khitan' or Western Liao, were one of history's great imperial re-foundations. When the Jurchens destroyed the Liao dynasty in North China, the Khitan prince Yelü Dashi refused surrender: with a few hundred followers he rode west across the steppe in 1124, rallied the tribes of Mongolia, and rebuilt an empire in Central Asia with its capital at Balasagun (in modern Kyrgyzstan), taking the title gurkhan, 'universal khan'.
para2: At their height the Kara Khitai ruled from the Oxus to the Altai: the Qarakhanid khanates of Kashgar and Samarkand, the Uyghurs, the Qarluks, and for a time the rising Khwarazmians all paid them tribute. Their decisive victory came at Qatwan, north of Samarkand (1141), where Yelü Dashi destroyed the army of the Seljuk sultan Sanjar - a battle that ended Seljuk power east of the Oxus and, in European retelling, grew into the legend of the Christian priest-king Prester John.
para3: The Kara Khitai kept the Liao dual system: Chinese-style administration and titles for the settled lands, steppe custom for the tribes. They were religiously plural - Buddhist Khitan rulers over mostly Muslim subjects, with Nestorian Christian, Jewish and shamanist communities - and Muslim writers praised their justice and the security of the trade routes under the gurkhans. Their rule preserved Central Asia's prosperity through the 12th century.
para4: The end came from within and without: the last gurkhans weakened the empire with wars against the rising Khwarazmshah, and in 1211 Kuchlug, a fugitive Naiman prince, usurped the throne and alienated the Muslim population with forced conversions. When Genghis Khan's general Jebe arrived in 1218, the cities surrendered without a fight. The Kara Khitai were forgotten in the West - except in the echo of their name: 'Cathay'.
