title: The Chagatai Khanate
titleline: The Chagatai Khanate - The History Web
para1: The Chagatai Khanate. The Chagatai Khanate (1227-1363) was the Central Asian quarter of the Mongol Empire, the ulus (appanage) of Chagatai, Genghis Khan's second son - a strict, traditional guardian of his father's law code (the Yasa), whose name the whole state bore. Stretching from the Oxus to the Altai, it was the most purely steppe-oriented of the Mongol khanates, and for decades the most turbulent: its khans rebelled repeatedly against the Great Khans, joining Kaidu's long war (1268-1301) against both the Yuan dynasty and the Ilkhanate.
para2: For much of the 13th century Transoxiana - the settled, Muslim, Persian-speaking land of Samarkand and Bukhara - suffered under khans who governed from the steppe and taxed the cities hard, while the khanate's eastern and western halves pulled apart. The turning point came with the 14th-century khans who settled in Transoxiana: Kebek (r. 1318-1326) built palaces and reformed the coinage, and Tarmashirin (r. 1326-1334) converted to Islam, provoking a steppe backlash that killed him and split the khanate in two - the Muslim west (Transoxiana) and the traditionalist east, Moghulistan.
para3: In the west, real power passed to the Turkic amirs - Qazaghan, then the Barlas clan - and in 1370 one of them, Timur (Tamerlane), took Samarkand, ruling behind puppet Chagatai khans as he built his own world empire. The eastern half, Moghulistan, survived under genuine Chagatai khans, raiding Timur and later splitting further; its last heir, Babur, driven out of Ferghana, went on to found the Mughal Empire of India (1526).
para4: The khanate's long shadow is linguistic and legal: the Turkic language of its realm, Chagatai, became the classical literary language of Central Asia down to the 19th century, and 'Chagatai' legitimacy - descent from Genghis Khan's second son - remained the coin of kingship from Timur's puppet khans to Babur's empire.

title: The Kingdom of Arakan
titleline: The Kingdom of Arakan - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Arakan. The Kingdom of Arakan (1429/1430-1785), with its capital at Mrauk U, ruled the narrow coastal strip of western Burma between the Arakan mountains and the Bay of Bengal - a frontier kingdom where Burmese, Bengali and maritime worlds met. Its golden age began when King Narameikhla (Min Saw Mon), restored from exile in Bengal with the help of the Bengal Sultanate, founded Mrauk U in 1430, acknowledging nominal Bengali suzerainty - a link that left Arakan's kings with Muslim-style titles and coins alongside their Buddhist ones.
para2: In the 16th-17th centuries Mrauk U was a power in the Bay of Bengal. Arakanese kings like Min Bin (r. 1531-1553) - who defended his kingdom against the Burmese conqueror Tabinshwehti and briefly occupied Chittagong - and their successors commanded fleets of fast galleys manned by Arakanese and Portuguese mercenaries, raiding deep into Bengal. The slave-trading port of Dianga and the Portuguese-tinged court of Mrauk U grew rich on rice, slaves, and the Bengal trade; the Flemish merchant Wouter Schouten and friar Sebastien Manrique left vivid accounts of the court.
para3: Mrauk U's cityscape still proclaims its power: tens of thousands of pagodas and massive fortress-like stone temples - the Shitthaung ('temple of 80,000 images') and Htukkanthein - built of dressed stone against the monsoon, unique in Burmese architecture. The court sponsored Pali scholarship and a distinctive Arakanese literature.
para4: Weakened by succession murders, Portuguese freebooting, and Mughal pressure from Bengal (which took Chittagong in 1666), the kingdom slid into a century of palace coups, and in 1785 the Burmese king Bodawpaya conquered it, carrying off its sacred Mahamuni Buddha image to Mandalay - a wound at the heart of Arakanese (Rakhine) identity to this day.
source3label: Britannica: Toungoo Dynasty

title: The Kingdom of Ava
titleline: The Kingdom of Ava - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Ava. The Kingdom of Ava (1364-1555) ruled the Irrawaddy heartland of Upper Burma from its capital at Ava (Inwa), on the river below Mandalay. Founded by Thado Minbya after the Mongol invasions had shattered the Pagan Empire, Ava fought a long 'Forty Years' War' (1385-1424) against the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy (Pegu) in the south for the mastery of Burma - an exhausting stalemate that defined two generations of Burmese and Mon history.
para2: Ava's kings presided over a flowering of Burmese culture even in wartime: the court made Burmese the language of high literature, produced great court poets and Buddhist scholarship, and maintained the intricate irrigation systems of the Kyaukse rice plain on which its power rested. But the kingdom was chronically weak at the center: its Shan vassal chiefs (sawbwas) of the northern hills grew ever more independent, and Ava survived by balancing them against each other and against the rising Shan state of Mogaung.
para3: In 1527 the Shan confederation under Sawlon of Mohnyin sacked Ava itself, and for three decades Upper Burma was ruled by Shan chiefs while the Burmese looked south to the rising power of Toungoo. In 1555 the Toungoo king Bayinnaung - the greatest conqueror in Burmese history - took Ava and reunified the country, and Ava became a provincial (though twice again royal) capital.
para4: Ava's four centuries made it the classical heartland of Burmese identity: the Burmese language, orthography, Theravada orthodoxy and court culture of later Burma were formed there, and its ruins at Inwa - walls, watchtower, monasteries - stand amid the rice fields south of Mandalay.

title: The Kingdom of Lan Xang
titleline: The Kingdom of Lan Xang - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Lan Xang. Lan Xang ('Land of a Million Elephants', 1353-1707) was the first kingdom of the Lao people and the ancestor of modern Laos. It was founded by Fa Ngum, a Lao prince raised at the Khmer court of Angkor, who returned with a Khmer army, conquered the Lao principalities of the Mekong valley, and was crowned at Luang Prabang in 1353, bringing with him Theravada Buddhism and the palladium of the kingdom - the Phra Bang, the gold Buddha image from which Luang Prabang takes its name.
para2: Under kings like Sam Sen Thai and Visoun in the 15th-16th centuries, Lan Xang held the middle Mekong against Vietnam, Ayutthaya and Burma, prospering on the river trade and forest products. The Burmese wars of the 1560s forced King Setthathirath to move his capital south to Vientiane (1560) - and to carry there the Phra Bang and the Emerald Buddha, the two great palladia of the Lao (the latter later seized by Siam and now in Bangkok). Setthathirath, builder of Vientiane's That Luang stupa, Laos' national monument, disappeared on campaign in 1571, and the kingdom fell into a half-century of succession struggles and Burmese interventions.
para3: Lan Xang's golden age came late, under Sourigna Vongsa (r. 1637-1694), whose long, stern and prosperous reign from Vientiane impressed the first European visitors - the Jesuit Leria and the Dutch merchant Van Wuysthoff - with the kingdom's wealth and discipline. But he died without naming an heir, and in 1707 Lan Xang split into three rival kingdoms - Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak - easy prey for Siam and Vietnam in the century that followed.
para4: Lan Xang remains the Lao nation's founding charter: the Phra Bang, the That Luang, and the memory of the million-elephant kingdom anchor Lao identity, and its 18th-century breakup explains both modern Laos' borders and its long subordination to Siam.
source3label: Britannica: Lan Xang

title: The Red Turban Rebellions
titleline: The Red Turban Rebellions - The History Web
para1: The Red Turban Rebellions. The Red Turban Rebellions (1351-1368) were the great uprisings that destroyed Mongol rule in China. By the 1340s the Yuan dynasty was rotting: floods of the Yellow River, famine, paper-money inflation, and the resentment of Chinese scholars and peasants at Mongol and Muslim privilege. In 1344 the river burst its banks and the dynasty conscripted 150,000 laborers to re-channel it - perfect tinder for revolt.
para2: The spark was the White Lotus, a Buddhist folk sect preaching the coming of Maitreya, the Buddha of the future, and the restoration of the Chinese Song dynasty. Its leaders Han Shantong - proclaimed the reincarnated Ming Wang ('King of Light') - and Liu Futong raised the standard in 1351, their armies wearing red headscarves that gave the movement its name. The Red Turbans soon split into two great movements: the northern, under Liu Futong and the child 'Little Prince' Han Lin'er, which retook Kaifeng and raided as far as the Yuan summer capital; and the southern, based in Hubei and the Yangzi valley.
para3: The Yuan could not cope: its own generals became warlords, and its chancellor Toghto, on the point of victory, was dismissed in a court intrigue (1354) and the imperial armies dissolved into rival camps. Into the vacuum stepped a Red Turban novice-monk turned warlord, Zhu Yuanzhang, who from his base at Nanjing systematically destroyed his rival rebel kings - Chen Youliang at the great lake battle of Poyang (1363), then Zhang Shicheng - and unified the south.
para4: In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang declared the Ming dynasty and marched north; the last Yuan emperor fled to the steppe, and Mongol rule over China ended after less than a century. The Red Turbans' legacy was double: the Ming dynasty itself, and a permanent Chinese fear and fascination with secret-society millenarian revolt.

title: The Sengoku Period
titleline: The Sengoku Period - The History Web
para1: The Sengoku Period. The Sengoku ('Warring States') period (1467-1615) was Japan's century and a half of total civil war. When the Onin War (1467-1477) destroyed both Kyoto and the Ashikaga shogunate's authority, real power dissolved into the hands of the sengoku daimyo - warlords who seized the provinces, built castle-towns, issued house laws, and fought endless wars of survival and conquest: the Takeda and Uesugi of the east, the Mori of the west, the Hojo of Odawara, the Imagawa, Oda and many more.
para2: The age remade Japanese war and society. Massed ashigaru (foot-soldier) armies of pikemen replaced samurai duels; castles grew from hill forts into the great stone keeps; and after the Portuguese landed at Tanegashima (1543), the daimyo adopted guns with astonishing speed - at Nagashino (1575) Oda Nobunaga's ranks of 3,000 arquebusiers destroyed the Takeda cavalry, the most famous volley in Japanese history. 'Gekokujo' - the low overthrowing the high - was the era's watchword, and talented men of humble birth could rise to rule provinces.
para3: Three unifiers ended the wars. Oda Nobunaga, from minor Owari, broke the old powers - burning the warrior-monks of Enryaku-ji, destroying the Takeda and the Ikko-ikki Buddhist leagues - and held central Japan when treachery killed him at Honno-ji (1582). His brilliant general Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a peasant's son, finished the unification (1590), froze the social order with his 'sword hunt', and died after two ruinous invasions of Korea (1592-1598). Tokugawa Ieyasu won the final contest at Sekigahara (1600), took the title shogun (1603), and eliminated the Toyotomi heir at Osaka Castle (1615).
para4: The Sengoku century bequeathed Japan its unified early-modern state, its castle cities, and its most celebrated heroes - Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu remain the benchmarks of Japanese leadership - while its wars burned out the old medieval order of court, temple and shugo for good.
source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Japanese Castles

title: The Malacca Sultanate
titleline: The Malacca Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Malacca Sultanate. The Malacca Sultanate (c. 1400-1511) was the greatest Malay commercial empire and the pivot of Asian trade in the 15th century. Its founder, Parameswara - a fugitive prince of Srivijaya from Palembang via Temasek (Singapore) - settled at the fishing village of Malacca around 1400, on the narrowest point of the strait that bears its name, the choke point of all shipping between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.
para2: Malacca's rise was deliberate and diplomatic: it protected traders, kept the strait free of pirates, standardized tolls and weights, and won the patronage of Ming China - Parameswara himself sailed to the Ming court, and Zheng He's treasure fleet used Malacca as a fortified depot. Merchants from Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Persia, Java, the Ryukyus and China crowded its port; one observer counted eighty-four languages spoken there, and the Venetian Suma Oriental called it the best market in the world.
para3: From mid-century Malacca became an empire and the engine of Islamization: its sultans - above all Mansur Shah (r. 1459-1477) - extended control over both shores of the strait and the tin-rich Malay interior; its royal chronicles, the Sejarah Melayu (Malay Annals), were composed at its court; and Islam, adopted by its rulers, spread with Malaccan trade and prestige to Java, Sumatra, Borneo, the Moluccas and the southern Philippines. Malay became the region's lingua franca.
para4: In 1511 the Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque stormed the city - the first European conquest in Southeast Asia - seeking to seize the spice trade at its source. The sultan fled to found the Johor dynasty, and Muslim trade partly shifted to Aceh and Johor, but Malacca's century had fixed the Malay world's religion, language, and royal ideal; its chronicles remain the charter myth of Malaysia.
source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Portuguese Malacca

title: The Demak Sultanate
titleline: The Demak Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Demak Sultanate. The Demak Sultanate (c. 1475-1554) was the first Muslim kingdom of Java and the agent of the island's Islamization. Founded on Java's north coast - traditionally by Raden Patah, a prince of mixed Chinese-Javanese or Majapahit descent, breaking from the declining Hindu-Buddhist empire of Majapahit - Demak grew rich on the rice and timber trade and on the fleets of the new Muslim merchant networks linking Java to Malacca and beyond.
para2: Demak's early sultans expanded aggressively: they took the Hindu ports of the north coast, raided Majapahit's heartland (the traditional date for Majapahit's final fall is 1527), and under Sultan Trenggana (r. 1504-1546) projected power across Java - against the Portuguese-backed Sundanese kingdom of Pajajaran in the west and into the eastern salient - while Demak's navy attacked Portuguese Malacca itself in 1513.
para3: The dynasty's memory is inseparable from the Wali Songo, the 'Nine Saints' revered as Java's apostles of Islam - preacher-traders like Sunan Ampel, Sunan Giri and Sunan Kudus, who founded mosques and pesantren schools and, in Javanese tradition, wove Islam into Javanese culture (wayang, gamelan, and the five-times prayer fitted to the gong cycle). Demak's Great Mosque, with its vast tiered roof and the mysterious saka guru pillars - one said to be of wood chips pressed by a saint - remains Java's holiest mosque.
para4: Trenggana's assassination in 1546 threw Demak into succession wars, and power passed to Pajang and then Mataram; the last Demak pretender was extinguished by 1554. But the sultanate had done its work: Java was Muslim, and the Wali Songo tradition it sponsored still defines Javanese Islam.
source3label: Britannica: Majapahit empire

article.p: The Demak Sultanate (c. 1475-1568) was the first Muslim kingdom of Java and the agent of the island's Islamization. It began as a small port fief of the Hindu-Buddhist empire of Majapahit on Java's north coast, founded in a marshy settlement called Glagah Wangi - traditionally by Raden Patah, a Javanese noble of the Majapahit royal line. When a usurper seized the Majapahit capital in 1478, Demak stopped sending tribute and declared itself independent, and nearly all the Muslim trading towns of the north coast followed. Rich on rice, timber and the fleets of the new Muslim merchant networks linking Java to Malacca and beyond, Demak became, for a century, the power that stood for Java itself.

article.h2: The Port That Stood for Java

article.p: Demak was a thalassocracy: its strength was its ships and its web of coastal cities. Raden Patah (r. 1475-1518) won hegemony over the trading ports of the north coast - Semarang, Jepara, Tuban and Gresik - and extended his overlordship to Jambi and Palembang in Sumatra, while his capital at the end of the channel separating Muria island from Java exported rice to Malacca and imported the spice trade's wealth. The Portuguese factor Tome Pires, writing in his Suma Oriental, judged that 'the Lord of Demak stood for all of Java'. The new sultanate made its faith visible: Raden Patah built the Great Mosque as the center of Islamic teaching and ruled with the saints of the Wali Songo at his side - Sunan Kudus as judge, Sunan Giri as mufti, Sunan Kalijaga as imam.

Demak fought to make its claim on Majapahit's inheritance real. From 1513 to 1518 it campaigned against Daha (Kediri), Majapahit's successor state in the interior, and destroyed it - Raden Patah died soon after the victory, in 1518. His successor Pati Unus (r. 1518-1521) threw the sultanate's fleets against the new foreign power in the region, leading two great expeditions against Portuguese Malacca - about a hundred ships in 1513 and 375 in 1521. Both failed, and Pati Unus was killed in the second, remembered ever since as Pangeran Sabrang Lor, 'the Prince who crossed to the North'. The throne then passed to Trenggana (r. 1521-1546), crowned by Sunan Gunungjati, the third and greatest ruler of Demak.

Trenggana answered the Portuguese threat by land. When the Portuguese allied with the Hindu Sundanese kingdom of Pajajaran in 1522, he sent his general Fatahillah - a Pasai-born veteran who had studied in Mecca - to take Sunda's ports: Banten and Sunda Kelapa fell in 1527, and Sunda Kelapa was renamed Jayakarta, the future Jakarta. Banten became a vassal sultanate under Hasanudin. Trenggana's armies rolled up the remaining Hindu resistance of central and eastern Java, conquered the last remnants of Majapahit itself and carried its royal heirlooms home to Demak. The expansion ended with him: campaigning against Pasuruan in East Java in 1546, he was assassinated - tradition says by a ten-year-old Duke of Surabaya with a kris, while serving the sultan betel nut.

article.p: Demak's memory is inseparable from the Wali Songo, the Nine Saints revered as Java's apostles of Islam. Preacher-traders like Sunan Ampel, Sunan Giri and Sunan Kudus founded mosques and pesantren schools up and down the coast and, in Javanese tradition, wove Islam into Javanese culture rather than breaking it - wayang puppetry, gamelan music and courtly custom were kept and given new meaning. Their monument still stands: Demak's Great Mosque, with its vast tiered roof and the saka guru pillars - one said to be of wood chips pressed together by a saint's hand - is widely held to be the oldest mosque in Indonesia, and the tombs of the saints and sultans around it still draw pilgrims.

Trenggana's murder unleashed a family blood feud. His son Sunan Prawata (Mukmin) took the throne in 1546, but in 1549 he was assassinated with the very kris he had used to kill his own uncle - by agents of Arya Penangsang of Jipang, the murdered uncle's son, who seized the throne. Penangsang's harshness turned the vassals against him: he had the queen of Jepara's husband killed, and she in turn demanded justice from Hadiwijaya of Pajang, Trenggana's son-in-law, better known as Jaka Tingkir. A coalition of vassals rose, and in 1568 Hadiwijaya's adopted son Sutawijaya - later the founder of Mataram - killed Penangsang. Hadiwijaya carried Demak's regalia and sacred heirlooms off to Pajang, and Demak sank to a vassal of the new power. The sultanate was finished, but its work was done: Java was Muslim, and the Wali Songo tradition it sponsored still defines Javanese Islam.

title: The Bengal Sultanate
titleline: The Bengal Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Bengal Sultanate. The Bengal Sultanate (1342-1576) ruled the wealthy delta of Bengal for two centuries as an independent Muslim kingdom. Bengal had been conquered in 1204 by the Ghurid general Bakhtiyar Khalji and governed from Delhi, but in 1342 the governor Shams al-Din Ilyas Shah broke away, unified the delta, and founded a dynasty whose successors - with one famous interruption - made Bengal one of the richest and most cosmopolitan states of the Indian Ocean.
para2: The interruption was extraordinary: Raja Ganesha, a Hindu zamindar of Dinajpur, seized effective power (1414-1418) and set his own son on the throne as the Muslim sultan Jalal al-Din Muhammad Shah - a Bengali convert under whom the sultanate took its distinctive syncretic form: Muslim kingship, Persian court culture, and deep patronage of the Bengali language. Under the restored Ilyas Shahi and then the Hussain Shahi dynasty (1494-1538) - whose founder, the Arab Alauddin Husain Shah, presided over Bengal's golden age - Bengali literature flowered with state support: the first great Bengali epics and Vaishnava poetry, and the building of Bengal's distinctive curved-eave mosques like the Sixty Dome Mosque of Bagerhat (a UNESCO site) and the great cities of Gaur and Pandua.
para3: Bengal's wealth was legendary: the delta's rice fed its dense population, and its muslins and silks, sugar and ships drew merchants from Malacca to Hormuz; the Portuguese established themselves at Chittagong and Hugli in the 16th century. The sultanate's coins circulated as far as Malacca, and its diplomatic correspondence ranged from the Mamluks to Ming China.
para4: Weakened by the Afghan (Suri) conquest of North India and by Arakanese and Portuguese pressure, the last sultans fell to the Mughals: Akbar's generals took Gaur, and after the defeat and death of Daud Khan Karrani (1576) Bengal became a Mughal province - the empire's richest, still remembered in Bengal as the end of its independent age.

title: The Kashmir Sultanate
titleline: The Kashmir Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Kashmir Sultanate. The Kashmir Sultanate (1320-1586) ruled the mountain-girdled Vale of Kashmir for over two and a half centuries. Founded when the last Hindu-Buddhist dynasty collapsed and Rinchana, a Buddhist prince from Ladakh converted to Islam, seized the throne (1320), it was consolidated by the Shah Mir dynasty, whose early sultans gave the valley its enduring character - above all Shihab al-Din (r. 1354-1373), who conquered the approaches to the valley and patronized its crafts.
para2: The sultanate's most beloved ruler was Zayn al-Abidin, 'Budshah' (the Great King, r. 1420-1470): he welcomed Persian scholars and artisans who made Srinagar a center of papier-mache, carpet-weaving, woodwork and shawl-making; he built canals and gardens; and - uniquely among the sultans of his age - he pursued a deliberate policy of tolerance, rebuilding Hindu temples, abolishing the jizya, and having the Hindu classics translated into Persian. Kashmiris of both faiths still remember Budshah as their ideal king.
para3: Under the sultans, Islam spread through the valley largely through the Sufi orders - the Rishis, Kashmir's own order of wandering ascetics founded by Sheikh Nur al-Din (Nund Rishi), revered by Muslims and Hindus alike, and the Kubrawi and Naqshbandi missionaries from Persia - creating Kashmir's distinctive blend of Persianate Islam and local Rishi tradition. Persian became the language of court and letters, which it remained for four centuries.
para4: After Budshah, factional wars between the Shah Mirs, their Chak successors - Shi'a soldiers who won the throne in 1561 - and rival noble clans exhausted the kingdom, and in 1586 the Mughal emperor Akbar annexed the valley. Kashmir's sultanate left the valley its religion, its crafts, its gardens and its identity as 'Paradise on Earth' - the image the Mughals would inherit and gild.

title: The Malla Kingdoms of Nepal
titleline: The Malla Kingdoms of Nepal - The History Web
para1: The Malla Kingdoms of Nepal. The Malla period (1200-1769) was the classical age of the Kathmandu Valley, when the Newar civilization of Nepal reached its artistic zenith. Founded by Ari Malla around 1200, the dynasty first ruled a unified valley kingdom, but from 1482 it split into three rival city-states - Kathmandu, Patan (Lalitpur), and Bhadgaon (Bhaktapur) - whose kings competed in war and, above all, in building: each city raised its own Durbar Square of palaces, tiered temples and gilded statues, today collectively a UNESCO World Heritage site.
para2: The Malla centuries gave Nepal its monuments and its culture. The valley's unique synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism deepened - Newar Buddhism with its own Sanskrit texts, monastic courtyards (bahals) and living goddess tradition (the Kumari, instituted by the Mallas) - while the Newar masters of wood, brick and bronze created the valley's signature style: multi-roofed pagoda temples, struts carved with deities, and bronzes exported as far as Tibet and China (the Nepali artist Araniko designed temples and stupas for Kublai Khan's Beijing).
para3: The rivalry of the three kingdoms - wars, alliances and espionage chronicled in the valley's own vamsavalis - kept the Mallas rich on the Tibet-India trade but politically divided. Kathmandu under Pratap Malla, Patan under Siddhi Narasimha, and Bhaktapur under Bhupatindra Malla (builder of the five-roofed Nyatapola temple, Nepal's tallest) each made their city a jewel of urban art.
para4: The division was fatal: in 1768-1769 Prithvi Narayan Shah, the ambitious king of the hill state of Gorkha, conquered the three cities one by one, unifying them into the modern kingdom of Nepal. The Mallas' cities remain the cultural heart of Nepal - their squares, festivals and the living Kumari still defining Kathmandu Valley life.

title: The Ahom Kingdom
titleline: The Ahom Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Ahom Kingdom. The Ahom Kingdom (1228-1826) ruled the Brahmaputra valley of Assam for six hundred years - one of the longest-lived dynasties in Indian history. Its founder, Sukaphaa, a Shan (Tai) prince from Mong Mao on the China-Burma border, crossed the Patkai mountains in 1228 with a small following, subdued and absorbed the local Barahi and Moran peoples, and planted a Tai state whose kings, administration (the paik labor system) and wet-rice agriculture organized the whole valley.
para2: The Ahoms' defining struggle was with Mughal India. Through the 17th century Mughal armies repeatedly invaded the valley, and repeatedly failed: the climactic battle of Saraighat (1671), where the Ahom general Lachit Borphukan's river-fleet destroyed a huge Mughal flotilla on the Brahmaputra, fixed India's northeast frontier for a century and made Lachit Assam's eternal hero. The Ahoms also absorbed the powerful Neo-Vaishnavite reform movement of Sankardev, whose satra monasteries reshaped Assamese religion, language and literature under royal patronage.
para3: Ahom Assam kept extraordinary records: the buranjis, chronicles written in the Ahom and later Assamese language on bark and aloe-bark paper, are among the finest historical traditions of premodern India. The kingdom's capital moved from Charaideo (whose pyramid-like royal tombs, the maidams, are a UNESCO site) to Gargaon and Rangpur, and its economy on wet rice, silk (muga), and the paik system of universal service.
para4: In the late 18th century the devastating Moamoria rebellions of the Mayamara sect broke the kingdom's strength; civil war brought Burmese invasions (1817-1826) that depopulated the valley, and in 1826 the British East India Company took Assam from Burma by the Treaty of Yandabo. The Ahoms left modern Assam its name (from 'Asam/Ahom'), its language's chronicles, and its distinct identity within India.

title: The Empire of Nicaea and the Byzantine Restoration
titleline: The Empire of Nicaea and the Byzantine Restoration - The History Web
para1: The Empire of Nicaea and the Byzantine Restoration. When the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204 and carved up the Byzantine Empire, three Greek successor states emerged - Trebizond, Epirus, and Nicaea - and it was Nicaea, across the Bosporus in northwest Asia Minor, that rebuilt Byzantium. Its founder, Theodore I Laskaris, the last emperor's son-in-law, organized the refugee government, church and army at Nicaea, was crowned emperor by a new patriarch (1208), and made his little state the magnet for Greeks who rejected the Latin Empire.
para2: Under Theodore's son-in-law John III Vatatzes (r. 1222-1254), Nicaea became a genuine imperial power: he crushed the Latin barons of Asia Minor, won over the Balkans from his Epirote rivals, took Thessalonica (1246), and ruled a disciplined, prosperous state whose army, treasury and learned court - he stocked libraries and schools - were the envy of the Greek world, remembered with affection as 'the Father of the Greeks'. His brief successor Theodore II, a scholar-emperor, prepared the restoration.
para3: The final act belonged to Michael VIII Palaiologos, an ambitious aristocrat who made himself regent and then co-emperor for the child John IV (whom he later blinded - a crime that shadowed his dynasty). In 1261 his general Alexios Strategopoulos retook Constantinople almost by accident with a handful of men, finding the Latin garrison away on a raid; on 15 August 1261 Michael entered the city in triumph and was crowned, restoring the Byzantine Empire after 57 years of Latin rule.
para4: Nicaea's legacy was double-edged: it preserved and restored Byzantium, its scholars (Blemmydes, Akropolites) led a Greek intellectual revival, and its diplomacy with Genoa (Treaty of Nymphaeum, 1261) outmaneuvered Venice - but Michael VIII's obsession with the west and the crusading threat left Asia Minor, the empire's old heartland, open to the Turks, who took it within a generation. The restored Palaiologan empire would linger, shrinking, until 1453.
